title: Chapter XXI
paragraphs: We had a difficult time with little Cathy that day. She woke in high spirits, eager to join her cousin. When she heard he had gone, she burst into such passionate tears and complaints that Edgar himself had to comfort her by promising Linton would soon return. He added, though, “if I can get him,” and there was no hope of that. The promise did little to soothe her, but time worked better. She still occasionally asked her father when Linton was coming back, yet before they met again, his face had faded so much in her memory that she did not recognise him.

Whenever business took me to Gimmerton and I happened to meet the Heights' housekeeper, I asked after the young master. He lived almost as secluded a life as Catherine and was never seen. From her I gathered that his health remained poor and that he was a troublesome member of the household. She said Mr. Heathcliff disliked him more and more, though he made some effort to hide it. He hated the sound of the boy's voice and could scarcely bear to sit in the same room with him for more than a few minutes. They seldom spoke much. Linton did his lessons and spent his evenings in a small room they called the parlour, or else lay in bed all day, for he was always catching coughs and colds or suffering from some ache or pain.

“I never knew such a timid creature,” the woman added, “nor one so careful of himself. The fuss he _will_ make if I leave a window open a little late in the evening! Oh! A breath of night air will kill him! He must have a fire in the middle of summer, and Joseph's tobacco pipe is poison, and he must always have sweets and dainties, and milk, milk, nothing but milk. Never a thought for how the rest of us suffer in winter. There he sits in his fur cloak beside the fire, with toast-water or some other slop warming on the hob for him to sip. If Hareton comes out of kindness to amuse him—and rough though Hareton is, he's not bad-hearted—they always part with one swearing and the other crying. I believe the master would enjoy Earnshaw beating him to a pulp if he weren't his son. And I'm certain he'd feel like turning him out if he knew half the fuss the boy makes over himself. But he keeps away from temptation. He never goes into the parlour, and if Linton starts those ways in the main room while he's there, he sends him straight upstairs.”

From this account I guessed that the complete absence of sympathy had made young Heathcliff selfish and disagreeable, if he had not been so already. My interest in him therefore lessened, although I still felt sorry for his fate and wished he had stayed with us. Mr. Edgar encouraged me to find out about him. I imagine he thought of him often and would have risked something to see him. Once he told me to ask the housekeeper whether the boy ever visited the village. She said he had ridden there with his father only twice, and each time claimed to be utterly exhausted for three or four days afterwards. If I remember correctly, that housekeeper left two years after his arrival. Another woman, whom I didn't know, replaced her and is still there.

Life at the Grange continued in its old pleasant way until Miss Cathy turned sixteen. We never celebrated her birthday, because it was also the anniversary of my late mistress's death. Her father always spent that day alone in the library. At dusk he walked to Gimmerton churchyard, often staying beyond midnight. Catherine therefore had to find her own entertainment. That twentieth of March was a beautiful spring day. Once her father had withdrawn, my young lady came downstairs dressed to go out and asked me to walk with her along the edge of the moor. Mr. Linton had given permission, provided we went only a short way and returned within an hour.
“So hurry, Ellen!” she cried. “I know where I want to go, to a place where some grouse live. I want to see whether they've built their nests yet.”
“That must be quite a way up,” I replied. “They don't nest at the edge of the moor.”
“No, it isn't,” she said. “I've been very close with papa.”

I put on my bonnet and went out without another thought. She bounded ahead, came back to my side, and darted away again like a young greyhound. At first I was well entertained by the larks singing near and far, the sweet warmth of the sunshine, and the sight of her, my darling and delight. Her golden curls streamed behind her; her bright cheek had the soft, pure bloom of a wild rose, and her eyes shone with untroubled joy. In those days she was a happy creature, and an angel. What a pity she couldn't remain content.
“Well, Miss Cathy,” I said, “where are your grouse? We ought to have reached them by now. We're a long way from the park fence.”
“Oh, just a little farther, Ellen,” she kept answering. “Climb that little hill, go past that bank, and by the time you're on the other side I'll have flushed the birds out.”

But there were so many hills and banks to climb and cross that I finally grew tired and told her we must stop and turn back. She was far ahead, so I shouted. Either she couldn't hear or she took no notice, for she kept bounding on and I had to follow. At last she dropped into a hollow. When I saw her again she was two miles closer to Wuthering Heights than to her own home. Two people had stopped her, and I was certain one was Mr. Heathcliff himself.
Cathy had been caught in the act of taking—or at least searching out—the nests of the grouse. Those heights belonged to Heathcliff, and he was scolding the poacher.

“I haven't taken any, or found any,” she said as I struggled up to them, spreading her hands to prove it. “I wasn't going to take them. Papa said there were lots up here, and I wanted to see the eggs.”
Heathcliff glanced at me with a malicious smile, showing that he knew who she was and therefore wished her ill, then asked who “papa” might be.
“Mr. Linton of Thrushcross Grange,” she replied. “I thought you couldn't know who I was, or you wouldn't have spoken like that.”
“So you suppose papa is greatly admired and respected?” he asked sarcastically.
“And who are you?” Catherine asked, studying him curiously. “I've seen that man before. Is he your son?”
She pointed to Hareton, his companion. The extra two years of his age had given him only greater size and strength. He looked as rough and awkward as ever.
“Miss Cathy,” I interrupted, “soon we'll have been out three hours instead of one. We really must go home.”

“No, that isn't my son,” Heathcliff answered, pushing me aside. “But I do have a son, and you've seen him before too. Though your nurse is in a hurry, I think a short rest would do you both good. Come round this little rise and into my house. A rest will get you home sooner, and you'll be warmly welcomed.”
I whispered to Catherine that she must not agree under any circumstances. It was completely out of the question.

“Why?” she asked aloud. “I'm tired from running, and the ground's wet with dew. I can't sit here. Let's go, Ellen. Besides, he says I've seen his son. I think he's mistaken, but I can guess where he lives: that farmhouse I visited on my way back from Penistone Crags. Isn't that right?”
“It is. Come, Nelly, keep quiet. She'll enjoy calling on us. Hareton, go ahead with the girl. You can walk with me, Nelly.”

“No, she isn't going there,” I cried, struggling to pull my arm free of his grasp. But she was almost at the doorstep already, having raced round the rise at full speed. Her appointed escort made no attempt to accompany her. He slipped off beside the road and disappeared.
“This is very wrong, Mr. Heathcliff,” I continued. “You know you mean no good. She'll see Linton there, and tell everything the moment we get home. I'll be the one blamed.”
“I want her to see Linton,” he answered. “He's been looking better these last few days. He isn't often fit to be seen. We'll soon persuade her to keep the visit secret. What harm is there in it?”
“The harm is that her father would hate me if he knew I'd let her enter your house,” I replied. “And I'm certain you've some bad purpose in encouraging her.”

“My purpose couldn't be more honest. I'll tell you exactly what it is,” he said. “I want the two cousins to fall in love and marry. I'm being generous to your master. His little chit has no prospects, and if she does as I wish, she'll be provided for at once as Linton's fellow heir.”
“If Linton died,” I answered, “and his life is far from certain, Catherine would inherit.”
“No, she wouldn't,” he said. “There's no clause in the will to ensure that. His property would come to me. But to avoid disputes, I want them married, and I'm determined to arrange it.”
“And I'm determined she shall never come near your house with me again,” I replied as we reached the gate where Miss Cathy was waiting.

Heathcliff told me to be quiet and hurried ahead up the path to open the door. My young lady looked at him several times, as though unable to decide what to think. But now he smiled whenever their eyes met and spoke to her gently. I was foolish enough to imagine that memories of her mother might keep him from wanting to hurt her. Linton stood by the hearth. He had been walking in the fields, for he still wore his cap and was calling Joseph to bring dry shoes. He had grown tall for his age, though he was still some months short of sixteen. His features remained pretty, and his eyes and complexion were brighter than I remembered, although it was only a temporary glow from the healthy air and warm sunshine.
“Now, who is this?” Mr. Heathcliff asked Cathy. “Can you tell?”
“Your son?” she said, looking uncertainly from one to the other.
“Yes, yes,” he answered. “But have you never seen him before? Think! Ah! What a short memory. Linton, don't you remember your cousin, whom you used to pester us so much to see?”
“What, Linton!” Cathy cried, lighting up with delighted surprise at the name. “Is this little Linton? He's taller than me! Are you really Linton?”

The boy stepped forward and said he was. She kissed him warmly, and each stared in wonder at how much the other had changed. Catherine had reached her full height. Her figure was both rounded and slender, springy as steel, and everything about her shone with health and energy. Linton looked and moved languidly and was extremely thin, but a certain grace in his manner softened these defects and made him quite pleasing. After many affectionate greetings, his cousin went over to Mr. Heathcliff. He lingered by the door, dividing his attention between indoors and outside—or pretending to watch outside while really watching only what went on within.

“So you're my uncle!” she cried, reaching up to kiss him. “I thought I liked you, even though you were cross at first. Why don't you bring Linton to visit the Grange? It's strange to live so close all these years and never see us. Why haven't you come?”
“I visited once or twice too often before you were born,” he answered. “There—damn it! If you've kisses to spare, give them to Linton. They're wasted on me.”

“Naughty Ellen!” Catherine cried, rushing to overwhelm me with kisses next. “Wicked Ellen, trying to stop me coming in! From now on I'll walk here every morning. May I, uncle? Sometimes I'll bring papa. Won't you be glad to see us?”

“Of course,” her uncle replied, scarcely suppressing a grimace at the thought of those two visitors, both of whom he deeply disliked. “But wait,” he continued, turning to her. “Now I think of it, I'd better explain. Mr. Linton is prejudiced against me. At one time we quarrelled with quite unchristian ferocity. If you tell him you've been here, he'll forbid your visits altogether. So don't mention it unless you don't care whether you see your cousin again. You may come if you wish, but you mustn't tell him.”
“Why did you quarrel?” Catherine asked, looking considerably downcast.
“He thought I was too poor to marry his sister,” Heathcliff answered, “and was upset when I did. It hurt his pride, and he'll never forgive it.”
“That's wrong!” the young lady said. “One day I'll tell him so. But Linton and I have nothing to do with your quarrel. Then I won't come here. He can visit the Grange.”
“It's too far for me,” her cousin murmured. “Walking four miles would kill me. No, Miss Catherine, come here now and then. Not every morning, but once or twice a week.”
His father shot him a look of bitter contempt.

“I'm afraid all my trouble will be wasted, Nelly,” he muttered to me. “‘Miss Catherine’, as the ninny calls her, will find out what he's worth and send him to the devil. Now, if it had been Hareton! Do you know, twenty times a day I wish Hareton were mine, degraded as he is? I'd have loved the lad if he had been someone else's. But I think he's safe from _her_ love. I'll set him against that paltry creature unless it makes a lively effort. We reckon it will scarcely live to eighteen. Oh, curse the spiritless thing! He's so busy drying his feet that he never looks at her. Linton!”
“Yes, father,” the boy answered.
“Have you nothing anywhere to show your cousin? Not even a rabbit or a weasel's nest? Before you change your shoes, take her into the garden, then to the stable to see your horse.”
“Wouldn't you rather stay here?” Linton asked Cathy, his voice plainly showing that he didn't want to move again.
“I don't know,” she answered, looking longingly towards the door, clearly eager to be doing something.

He stayed seated and drew closer to the fire. Heathcliff got up, went through the kitchen into the yard, and called Hareton. Hareton answered, and soon they both came in. The young man had washed: his glowing cheeks and wet hair made that plain.
“Oh, I'll ask _you_, uncle,” Miss Cathy cried, remembering what the housekeeper had said. “He isn't my cousin, is he?”
“Yes,” he replied. “Your mother's nephew. Don't you like him?”
Catherine made an odd face.
“Isn't he a handsome lad?” Heathcliff went on.

The rude little creature stood on tiptoe and whispered something in his ear. He laughed; Hareton's face darkened. I saw that he was very sensitive to anything that seemed like a slight, and plainly had a vague sense of being inferior. But his master or guardian drove away his frown by exclaiming:

“You'll be everyone's favourite, Hareton! She says you're a—what was it? Well, something very flattering. Here! Take her round the farm. And mind you behave like a gentleman! No bad language. Don't stare when she isn't looking, then hide your face when she is. Speak your words slowly, and keep your hands out of your pockets. Off you go, and entertain her as well as you can.”

He watched them pass the window. Earnshaw had turned his face completely away from his companion. He seemed to be studying the familiar landscape with the interest of a stranger or an artist. Catherine gave him a sly glance that showed little admiration. Then she looked for ways to amuse herself and skipped merrily along, singing a tune to make up for the lack of conversation.

“I've tied his tongue,” Heathcliff observed. “He won't dare say a word the whole time! Nelly, you remember me at his age—no, some years younger. Did I ever look so stupid, so ‘gawmless’, as Joseph would say?”
“Worse,” I replied, “because you were more sullen as well.”

“He gives me pleasure,” Heathcliff went on, thinking aloud. “He's fulfilled my expectations. If he'd been born a fool, I wouldn't enjoy it half as much. But he isn't a fool, and I can understand all his feelings because I've felt them myself. I know exactly what he's suffering now, for instance, though it's only the beginning of what he's going to suffer. And he'll never climb out of his pit of coarseness and ignorance. I've trapped him more securely, and lower down, than his scoundrel father trapped me, because he's proud of his brutishness. I've taught him to despise everything beyond animal life as foolish and weak. Don't you think Hindley would be proud of his son if he could see him? Almost as proud as I am of mine. But there's a difference. One is gold used for paving stones; the other is tin polished to look like silverware. _Mine_ has nothing valuable in him, yet I'll deserve credit for making such poor material go as far as it can. _His_ had first-rate qualities, and they've been lost—made worse than useless. _I_ have nothing to regret. _He_ would have more than anyone but me knows. And the best part is that Hareton is damnably fond of me! You must admit I've beaten Hindley there. If that dead villain rose from his grave to abuse me for what I've done to his son, I'd have the pleasure of watching the son fight him back into it, outraged that he should insult the only friend he has in the world!”

Heathcliff chuckled devilishly at the thought. I didn't reply, seeing that he expected no answer. Meanwhile our young companion, sitting too far away to hear us, grew restless. He probably regretted giving up Catherine's company to avoid a little exertion. His father noticed his uneasy glances towards the window and his hand reaching uncertainly for his cap.
“Get up, you lazy boy!” he exclaimed with false heartiness. “Go after them! They're just round the corner, beside the beehives.”

Linton summoned his strength and left the fire. The window was open. As he went outside, I heard Cathy asking her unsociable guide about the inscription over the door. Hareton looked up and scratched his head like a proper country lout.
“Some damned writing,” he answered. “I can't read it.”
“You can't read it?” Catherine cried. “I can. It's English. I wanted to know why it's there.”
Linton giggled, showing amusement for the first time.
“He doesn't know his letters,” he told his cousin. “Can you believe anyone could be such an enormous dunce?”

“Is he quite as he ought to be?” Miss Cathy asked seriously. “Or is he simple—not right in his mind? I've asked him two questions, and each time he looked so stupid I thought he couldn't understand me. I'm sure I can hardly understand _him_!”
Linton laughed again and gave Hareton a taunting glance. At that moment Hareton certainly seemed less than clear about what was happening.

“There's nothing wrong except laziness, is there, Earnshaw?” he said. “My cousin thinks you're an idiot. That's what comes of despising ‘book-learning’, as you'd call it. Have you noticed his dreadful Yorkshire pronunciation, Catherine?”

“What t' devil's the use of it?” Hareton growled, finding his tongue more easily with his everyday companion. He was about to say more, but the two young people burst into loud laughter. My thoughtless young lady was delighted to discover that his strange speech could amuse her.
“What use is the devil in that sentence?” Linton tittered. “Papa told you not to use bad language, and you can't open your mouth without it. Do try to behave like a gentleman, please!”

“If thou weren't more lass than lad, I'd knock thee down this minute, I would, thou pitiful stick of a creature!” the angry young rustic retorted. He retreated, his face burning with rage and humiliation. He knew he was being insulted, but did not know how to answer it.

Mr. Heathcliff had heard the conversation as clearly as I had. He smiled as Hareton went away, then immediately gave the flippant pair still chatting in the doorway a look of extraordinary disgust. The boy found plenty of energy to discuss Hareton's faults and shortcomings and tell stories about his behaviour. The girl enjoyed his cheeky, spiteful remarks without considering the unkindness they revealed. I began to dislike Linton more than I pitied him, and to excuse his father to some degree for thinking so little of him.

We stayed until afternoon; I could not get Miss Cathy away sooner. Luckily my master had not left his room and knew nothing of our long absence. On the walk home I tried to explain the characters of the people we had just left. But she had decided I was prejudiced against them.

“Aha!” she cried. “You take papa's side, Ellen. I know you're biased, or you wouldn't have deceived me all these years into thinking Linton lived far away. I'm really very angry, only I'm too pleased to show it! But you must keep quiet about my uncle. Remember, he's _my_ uncle, and I'll scold papa for quarrelling with him.”

She went on like this until I gave up trying to show her she was mistaken. She said nothing about the visit that evening, because she didn't see Mr. Linton. Next day it all came out, much to my dismay. Still, I wasn't entirely sorry. I thought he would guide and warn her more effectively than I could. But he was too hesitant about explaining fully why he wanted her to avoid everyone at the Heights, and Catherine demanded good reasons for anything that checked her indulged will.

“Papa!” she exclaimed after greeting him that morning. “Guess who I met on the moors yesterday. Ah, papa, you jumped! You haven't behaved properly, have you? I saw—but listen, and I'll tell you how I found you out. And Ellen too, who's been in league with you while pretending to feel so sorry for me whenever I hoped Linton would return and was disappointed again!”

She gave an accurate account of her outing and what followed. My master cast several reproachful glances at me but said nothing until she finished. Then he drew her close and asked whether she knew why he had hidden the fact that Linton lived nearby. Could she think he wanted to deny her a pleasure that would do her no harm?
“It was because you disliked Mr. Heathcliff,” she replied.

“Then you believe my own feelings matter more to me than yours, Cathy?” he said. “No. It wasn't because I dislike Mr. Heathcliff, but because he dislikes me. He's a devilish man who delights in hurting and ruining people he hates whenever they give him the slightest chance. I knew you couldn't remain friends with your cousin without meeting him, and I knew he would hate you because of me. So I took care to prevent your seeing Linton again entirely for your own good. I meant to explain when you were older, and I'm sorry I waited.”

“But Mr. Heathcliff was very friendly, papa,” Catherine said, quite unconvinced. “_He_ didn't object to our seeing each other. He said I could visit whenever I liked, only I mustn't tell you because you'd quarrelled with him and wouldn't forgive him for marrying Aunt Isabella. And you won't. _You're_ the one to blame. At least he's willing to let _us_ be friends, Linton and me, and you aren't.”

Seeing that she would not simply accept his word about her uncle by marriage, my master briefly described Heathcliff's treatment of Isabella and how he had acquired Wuthering Heights. He could not bear to discuss it for long. Though he rarely spoke of it, he still felt the same horror and hatred of his old enemy that had filled his heart since Mrs. Linton's death. “She might still be alive if it weren't for him!” was his constant bitter thought. In his eyes, Heathcliff was a murderer. Miss Cathy knew no wrongdoing beyond her own small acts of disobedience, unfairness, and anger, born of a hot temper and thoughtlessness and regretted the same day. She was astonished that a mind could be so dark as to brood secretly over revenge for years and deliberately carry out its plans without remorse. This new picture of human nature, absent until now from everything she had studied or imagined, seemed to shock her so deeply that Mr. Edgar thought further explanation unnecessary. He only added, “Later you'll understand, darling, why I want you to avoid his house and family. For now, go back to your usual work and pleasures, and think no more about them.”

Catherine kissed her father and quietly settled to her lessons for the usual couple of hours. Afterwards she walked with him in the grounds, and the day passed as normal. But that evening, when I went to her room to help her undress, I found her kneeling beside the bed in tears.

“Oh, shame, you silly child!” I cried. “If you had real troubles, you'd be ashamed to waste a tear over this little disappointment. You've never known even the shadow of genuine sorrow, Miss Catherine. Imagine for a moment that your father and I were dead and you were alone in the world. How would you feel then? Compare this with a grief like that, and be grateful for the friends you have instead of wanting more.”
“I'm not crying for myself, Ellen,” she answered. “I'm crying for him. He expects to see me tomorrow, and he'll be so disappointed. He'll wait for me, and I won't come!”

“Nonsense!” I said. “Do you think he's thought about you as much as you've thought about him? Doesn't he have Hareton for company? Not one person in a hundred would cry over losing a relation they'd only seen twice, for two afternoons. Linton will guess what's happened and think no more about you.”

“But couldn't I write a note explaining why I can't come?” she asked, getting up. “And send the books I promised to lend him? His aren't as nice as mine, and when I told him how interesting mine were, he wanted them very much. Couldn't I, Ellen?”

“No, indeed! Certainly not!” I replied firmly. “Then he'd write back, and it would never end. No, Miss Catherine, you must have no more contact with him. That's what papa expects, and I'll make sure of it.”
“But how could one little note—?” she began again, putting on a pleading expression.
“Be quiet!” I interrupted. “We aren't starting with your little notes. Get into bed.”

She gave me such a naughty look that at first I refused to kiss her good night. I tucked her in and closed the door, thoroughly displeased. Halfway away, though, I relented and went quietly back. And there she was, standing at the table with a sheet of blank paper before her and a pencil in her hand! She guiltily hid the pencil as I entered.
“If you write that, Catherine, you won't find anyone to deliver it,” I said. “And now I'm putting out your candle.”

I lowered the snuffer over the flame and received a slap on the hand and an angry “Cross thing!” for my pains. Then I left again, and she bolted the door in one of her worst, most petulant moods. She finished the letter and sent it through a boy who collected milk for the village, though I did not discover that until later. Weeks passed, and Cathy's good temper returned. But she became remarkably fond of slipping into corners alone. If I suddenly approached while she was reading, she often started and bent over her book, plainly trying to hide it. I noticed loose sheets of paper sticking out between the pages. She also took to coming downstairs early and lingering in the kitchen, as though expecting something to arrive. She had a small drawer in a library cabinet over which she would spend hours, and she was particularly careful to take its key whenever she left.

One day, while she was looking through the drawer, I saw that the toys and trinkets it had lately held had turned into folded pieces of paper. Curious and suspicious, I decided to examine these mysterious treasures. That night, once she and my master were safely upstairs, I searched among my household keys and easily found one that fitted. I opened the drawer, emptied everything into my apron, and carried it to my own room to inspect at leisure. Despite my suspicions, I was still surprised to find a mass of letters from Linton Heathcliff. They must have written almost daily: these were replies to letters she had sent him. The earliest were awkward and short. Gradually they became lengthy love letters, as foolish as the writer's age made natural, yet with occasional touches I thought borrowed from someone more experienced. Some struck me as very strange mixtures of passion and dullness, beginning with strong feeling and ending in the affected, wordy style a schoolboy might use to an imaginary sweetheart. Whether they satisfied Cathy I cannot say. To me they seemed worthless rubbish. After reading as many as I thought necessary, I tied them in a handkerchief, set them aside, and locked the empty drawer again.

As usual, my young lady came down early and went to the kitchen. I watched her go to the door when a certain little boy arrived. While the dairymaid filled his can, Cathy slipped something into his jacket pocket and took something out. I went round through the garden and waited for the messenger. He fought bravely to protect his charge, and between us we spilt the milk, but I managed to seize the letter. After threatening dire consequences unless he hurried home, I stayed beside the wall and read Miss Cathy's affectionate composition. It was simpler and more eloquent than her cousin's, very pretty and very silly. I shook my head and went thoughtfully indoors. Since it was raining, she couldn't amuse herself in the park. When her morning lessons ended, she turned to the drawer for comfort. Her father sat reading at the table, and I had deliberately found work repairing some loose curtain fringe so I could keep watch. No bird returning to a robbed nest it had left full of chirping young could have shown greater despair in its cries and fluttering than she showed in one “Oh!” and the transformation of her previously happy face. Mr. Linton looked up.
“What's wrong, love? Have you hurt yourself?” he asked.
His voice and expression reassured her that _he_ had not found her treasure.
“No, papa!” she gasped. “Ellen! Ellen! Come upstairs. I feel ill!”
I did as she asked and went out with her.

“Oh, Ellen! You've got them,” she began at once, falling to her knees as soon as we were alone. “Oh, give them back, and I'll never, never do it again! Don't tell papa. You haven't told him, Ellen? Say you haven't! I've been terribly naughty, but I won't do it any more!”
With a solemn, stern manner I ordered her to stand.

“So, Miss Catherine,” I exclaimed, “you seem to have gone quite far! You ought to be ashamed of them. What a fine bundle of rubbish you study in your spare time—good enough to print! What do you think the master will say when I show it to him? I haven't yet, but don't imagine I'll keep your ridiculous secrets. Shame on you! You must have started writing this nonsense. I'm sure he wouldn't have thought of it first.”
“I didn't! I didn't!” Cathy sobbed as though her heart would break. “I never thought of loving him until—”

“_Loving_!” I cried, putting all the scorn I could into the word. “_Loving_! Who ever heard of such a thing! I might as well talk of loving the miller who comes once a year to buy our grain. Fine love, indeed! You've barely spent four hours with Linton in your life, counting both visits! Now, here's the childish nonsense. I'm taking it to the library, and we'll see what your father thinks of such _love_.”

She sprang towards her precious letters, but I held them above my head. Then she begged frantically that I burn them, do anything rather than show them. I was really as inclined to laugh as to scold, since I considered it all girlish vanity. At last I softened a little and asked, “If I agree to burn them, will you solemnly promise never to send or receive another letter, or a book—I see you've sent him books—or locks of hair, rings, or toys?”
“We don't send toys,” Catherine cried, her pride getting the better of her shame.
“Nor anything at all, then, my lady?” I said. “Unless you promise, I'm going.”
“I promise, Ellen!” she cried, catching my dress. “Oh, put them in the fire, please, please!”
But when I began making a space in the fire with the poker, the sacrifice became too painful to bear. She begged me earnestly to spare one or two.
“One or two, Ellen, to keep for Linton's sake!”
I untied the handkerchief and began tipping them into the fire from one corner. Flames curled up the chimney.
“I will have one, you cruel wretch!” she screamed. She plunged her hand into the fire and pulled out some half-burnt scraps, burning her fingers in the process.
“Very well, then I'll keep some to show papa!” I answered. I shook the rest back into the bundle and turned towards the door again.

She dropped her blackened scraps into the flames and motioned for me to finish the sacrifice. I did so, stirred the ashes, and buried them beneath a shovelful of coal. Silent and feeling deeply wronged, she went to her own room. I went downstairs and told my master that the young lady's sudden sickness had almost passed, but I thought she should lie down for a while. She refused dinner. At tea she reappeared, pale and red-eyed, with an outward meekness quite unlike her. Next morning I answered the letter with a slip of paper: “Master Heathcliff is asked to send no more notes to Miss Linton, as she will not accept them.” After that, the little boy's pockets came empty.
